messages.content: You are the neutral rapporteur of a technology readiness review panel. Consolidate, attribute and preserve disagreement; do not decide and do not add technical claims of your own.

# Synthesis: assess · T13

## Claude Opus 5.5


# TRL assessment: T13, asteroid water extraction pilot (`isru-water-extraction`)

## 0. Scope and what changed since March 2026

**What is rated.** The rating covers the integrated chain that turns C-type regolith into stored, purified liquid water at an NEA:

feed acquisition → containment → thermal dehydration → vapour capture → purification → storage

The required output is 10–100 t/yr of water.

**What is not rated.** Electrolysis, LOX/LH₂ and water-EP thrusters are outside this technology. The revised architecture rules out production propellant in Phase 0. Rq-0-33 (microgravity electrolysis) therefore does not bear on this rating. It matters only if rq-0-55 later selects a water-EP route that needs electrolysis, and most water-EP concepts (resistojet, electrothermal, RF/plasma) do not.

**Three corrections to the March entry.**
1. **Target TRL 7 and "project-ending" no longer apply.** The 0B product is Fe-Ni, and the tugs are iodine or argon (D-05). Nothing in the 0B baseline consumes water.
2. **The lunar-poles fallback contradicts the architecture.** There is no production propellant in Phase 0, so there is nothing for lunar water to substitute for.
3. **Two items in the evidence list are not technology evidence.** The Paper 05 Monte Carlo is a design study, so it cannot support TRL ≥ 3. The Bennu sample is evidence about the *resource* and the feed mineralogy, not about *extraction*.

**Site implication (Claude's condition).** CI and CM chondrites carry almost no native Fe-Ni. A C-type pilot is therefore almost certainly a separate site, with its own:
- power (estimated 5–200 kWth, below);
- feed handling and containment;
- debris licence under D-03.

The only plausible co-location case is a CR-like body, which is both metal-bearing and hydrated, but carries less water. I assign a low prior to finding one among accessible NEAs. This is my judgement, not a survey result.

**Working assumptions.** The inputs do not state these, so they are mine:

| Quantity | Assumed value | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Recoverable water yield | 4–12 wt% of feed | Heating to ~400–800 °C. The total H₂O-equivalent in CI material is higher, but not all of it is recoverable at practical temperatures without excessive SO₂/CO₂ co-release. |
| Feed | ~80–2,500 t/yr (≈0.2–7 t/day averaged) | Follows from the yield and the 10–100 t/yr output |
| Thermal energy | ~10–20 MJ/kg water before losses; 15–60 MJ/kg with losses | Sensible heat ≈0.5–0.7 MJ/kg ore, plus dehydroxylation of the order of a few MJ/kg water |
| Average thermal power | ~5–200 kWth | Peak is higher at a 9–25% duty cycle |
| Duration | ≥1 yr continuous campaign within a 3–5 yr site life | Not specified in the requirement |

**Purpose (Claude) and purity specification (GPT).** Neither is defined. This matters directly for the rating, because the TRL 4 exit criterion requires a "documented definition of the relevant environment". In practice that includes the feed specification and the product specification. Neither exists.

---

## 1. Evidence

| E2 | Ryugu is CI-like and dominated by phyllosilicates | Yokoyama et al., 2023, *Science* (Hayabusa2 return) | ~5.4 g returned; lab analysis | n/a (resource) | Yes |

The figure of "10%+ water" in the March entry is unverified by me. |
| E4 | Soluble evaporite salts (Na carbonates, phosphates, sulfates and others) in Bennu | McCoy et al., 2025, *Nature* | Lab analysis of returned grains | n/a. Relevant to purification: salts and anions in condensate and fines. | Yes on existence. Details moderate. |

| E6 | Bennu's surface is very weakly bound and behaved fluid-like during TAG | Lauretta et al., 2022, *Science*; Walsh et al., 2022, *Science Advances* | Spacecraft contact event at a real NEA | n/a. Bears on feed acquisition and containment design. | Yes |
| E7 | CI/CM asteroid simulants with documented mineralogy | Britt et al., 2019, *Meteoritics & Planetary Science* (UCF/Exolith) | Bulk simulant supply | n/a (test-feed enabler). Organics, NH₃ and evaporite content are probably not representative of Bennu. | Yes on existence. Representativeness is my judgement. |
| E8 | Water extracted from asteroid simulant in vacuum and used as steam propellant (WINE hopper concept) | Honeybee Robotics with UCF, ~2018–2019 | Grams of water, lab vacuum chamber, 1 g | 10–100 t/yr ÷ grams per test ≈ 10⁵–10⁷ (rate not well defined) | **No.** Programme recalled; mass and rate figures not confirmed. |
| E9 | Optical mining (concentrated sunlight) spalls and devolatilises CI simulant | Sercel et al., NASA NIAC Phase I/II (APIS), ~2016–2019 | Lab vacuum, kg-class or smaller simulant. "8 kW" from the March entry not confirmed. | ≥10³–10⁵ | **No** on test scale and power |
| E10 | Physics-based thermal model of volatile extraction | Metzger et al. (cited as arXiv 2306.03776, with Zacny and Morrison) | Analysis only | n/a. Analysis is not TRL evidence unless validated against test data. | **No** on exact authorship and ID as cited |
| E11 | Long-duration microgravity water purification and distillation | ISS Water Recovery System (WPA/UPA), operational since 2008–2009 | Order of a few t/yr, ISS cabin and urine feed chemistry, microgravity, years | ~1–30× on throughput. Feed chemistry differs: SO₂, H₂S, CO₂, NH₃, organics, salts, fines. | Yes on the programme. Throughput is approximate. |
| E12 | In-situ chemical processing on another body, autonomous, repeated runs | MOXIE on Perseverance, 2021–2023 (Hecht et al., 2021, *Space Sci. Rev.*; Hoffman et al., 2022, *Sci. Adv.*) | ~6–12 g/h O₂ from CO₂, a different process | Indirect only (operations heritage, not water) | Yes |
| E13 | Passive magnetic gas–liquid separation for microgravity electrolysis | Romero-Calvo, Brinkert, Akay et al., 2025, *Nature Chemistry* (drop tower) | Lab cell, seconds of microgravity | **Out of scope** for this pilot | Moderately |

### What the evidence does and does not show

**Not demonstrated anywhere, to my knowledge:**
- continuous processing of hydrated regolith at the required rate;
- operation under vacuum *and* in microgravity;
- vapour capture from an open or partially sealed granular bed in microgravity;
- fines-laden condensate purification to a stated specification;
- runs on feed with representative organic, sulfur and salt chemistry, rather than only on simulant.

**On the related research questions:**
- **Rq-0-40.** Its literature review frames volatile loss as ice sublimation. That is largely misdirected for an NEA at ~1 AU, where the water is in phyllosilicates and is stable to several hundred °C. Frictional excavation heating is a second-order loss for bound water, though loosely adsorbed water may be lost early. The Interamnia ice result it cites concerns a main-belt body and does not apply to NEAs.
- **Rq-0-33.** Its "500–750 kW" figure is from the abandoned architecture.

---

## 2. Current TRL: 3–4

The rating splits by element.

| Element | TRL | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Dehydration chemistry and yield prediction | 3, approaching 4 | E1 and E7 provide experimental results that validate the key parameter (water release versus temperature) |
| Integrated feed-handling, capture and purification chain | 3 at best | No breadboard has been tested against predictions on a defined feed |

**Lower bound, TRL 3: met.** The TRL 3 exit criterion is "documented experimental results validating predictions of key parameters". E1 meets it on water release versus temperature for real meteorites, supported by simulant work (E7) and small vacuum demos (E8, E9).

**Unmet for TRL 4 (at the lower bound). Three gaps:**
1. **No breadboard test on a defined feed.** There is no documented breadboard extractor, run on feed of defined mineralogy, whose yield and condensate composition agree with prediction. The simulants used likely lack Bennu-like organic, NH₃ and evaporite content.
2. **No product specification.** There is no documented definition of the relevant environment *including* the purity specification. This cannot exist until the pilot's purpose is stated.
3. **No purification breadboard.** None has been validated on CI-derived condensate.

**Upper bound, TRL 4.** This is credible only if E8 and E9 are accepted as breadboard validation of the extraction step alone. Even then, two criteria remain unmet:
- **For TRL 5:** a component or breadboard validated in the relevant environment. Nothing has been tested combining vacuum, microgravity granular handling and containment, thermal cycling at 0.9–1.3 AU, and charged abrasive fines over meaningful duration. Parabolic and drop-tower time (seconds) is too short for a heat-up, dehydration and capture cycle.
- **For TRL 5:** a documented definition of scaling requirements.

**Scale gap.**
- The best demonstrated rates I can confirm are grams to perhaps kg per test.
- The required rate is ~0.2–7 t/day of feed.
- The gap is therefore roughly **10²–10⁴ on rate**, with no continuous-duration demonstration at all.

---

## 3. Target and difficulty

**Target TRL at KDP-0B: 5.** The reasoning under D-02:
- The pilot is not project-ending for 0B, so TRL 6 without waivers is not required.
- The internal-milestone band of 4–5 applies.
- Because the KDP-0B decision is to *commit a flight pilot*, I set the top of that band.
- The pilot then functions as the TRL 6–7 demonstration at reduced scale.

**Escalation clause.** If rq-0-55 selects water EP as a Phase 1 transport route, water becomes project-critical and the target rises to **TRL 6 at KDP-0B**.

**Needed by.** KDP-0B. The inputs give no date; I assume roughly 2031–2034. Two conditions precede it:
- a C-type target sampled under the D-02 target gate;
- a written purpose and purity specification, which should be in hand by the 0A mid-term review.

**AD² = 5** (new development, not done before, path clear, ~70% success).
- The chemistry is understood and the process steps (oven, cold trap, staged purification) are conventional.
- Microgravity granular containment and vapour capture from a fines-laden bed have never been done, so AD² 4 overstates heritage.
- **For a step to TRL 6 the rating would be AD² 6.** Three routes compete with no clear winner: excavate-and-oven, optical mining, and in-place bagged or capped heating. Each has a different failure mode: seal and abrasion, optics fouling, and capture efficiency respectively.

---

## 4. Path

| # | Step | Method | Scale | Cost (US$) | Duration | Reaches TRL |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | State the purpose and derive the product specification: water-EP test feed, Phase 1 option, or science/prospecting. Set yield and purity targets per purpose. | Analysis | Programme | 0.5–2 M | 0.5–1 yr | Prerequisite for the TRL 4 exit |
| P2 | Compile evolved-gas and TGA data for CI/CM/CR meteorites, Ryugu and Bennu. Request a mg-scale curation allocation for Bennu EGA if not already published. Build a feed model covering H₂O, CO₂, SO₂/H₂S, NH₃, organics and salts versus temperature. | Literature + experiment | mg | 0.3–1.5 M | 1–2 yr | 3 (firmed) |
| P3 | Develop simulant with representative organics, sulfides, sulfates and evaporites; cross-check against P2. | Experiment | 100 kg–1 t batches | 1–4 M | 1–2 yr | Enabler |
| P4 | Bench extractor in thermal-vacuum: batch runs at 1–10 kg, then continuous at 10–50 kg/day. Measure yield against prediction, condensate speciation and fines carryover. Run oven and optical variants head-to-head. | Experiment | 10–50 kg/day | 5–20 M | 2–3 yr | 4 |
| P5 | Purification breadboard: staged cold-trap fractionation, sorbents, distillation and ion exchange, run against the P1 specification on P4 condensate. Reuse ISS WRS heritage where applicable. | Experiment | 0.1–1 t/yr water | 2–8 M | 1–2 yr | 4 |
| P6 | Reduced-gravity granular handling, sealing and capture. Use parabolic or drop tower for flow and seal physics, then an ISS or free-flyer payload processing kg-scale charged simulant over weeks. | Experiment | kg, weeks | 10–60 M | 2–4 yr | 5 |
| P7 | Thermal model validation: calibrate the extraction and loss model against P4 and P6 data, and document the scaling requirements needed for the TRL 5 exit. | Simulation | Full pilot range | 0.5–2 M | 1 yr (in parallel) | 5 (exit documentation) |
| P8 | *(Only if escalated to TRL 6.)* Integrated subsystem prototype at 0.1–1 t/day feed for ≥1,000 h in thermal-vacuum with abrasive fines. Microgravity behaviour bounded by P6. | Experiment | 0.1–1 t/day | 50–200 M | 3–5 yr | 6 |
| P9 | *(Optional, 0A.)* kg-scale extraction payload on a C-type rendezvous scout (200–600 kg class). This is the only route to real-feed, real-environment data before KDP-0B. | Experiment (flight) | kg to tens of kg | 50–150 M incremental | 4–7 yr | 6–7 at small scale (remaining scale gap ~10³) |

**Totals.**
- Path to TRL 5 (P1–P7): about **US$20–100 M over 3–6 years**.
- Path to TRL 6, if escalated: add P8 or P9, giving **US$70–300 M**.

---

## 5. Risk and fallback

**Risk if it fails to reach target: cost-increase.**
- No 0B baseline element depends on water. The Fe-Ni product, the iodine/argon tugs and the uncrewed operations all proceed without it.
- What is lost is the option value of in-space water, plus any sunk R&D.
- This becomes **architecture-change** only if rq-0-55 makes water EP part of the Phase 1 transport plan.

**Fallback.** Drop or defer the pilot:
- keep the iodine/argon tug reference (D-05);
- hold water extraction at ground TRL 4 as a Phase 1 option;
- if water is ever needed in Phase 0, supply it from Earth in tonne quantities.

Lunar polar water is not a meaningful fallback under the revised architecture.

---

## 6. Where others might disagree

1. **Should the pilot be in Phase 0 at all?** I tag it 0B (conditional) because the architecture names it. A stricter reading of Claude's "purpose to be stated" and GPT's analysis in rq-0-55 would tag it **deferred**: with no customer, a separate site and its licence are hard to justify. I would accept "deferred" if no purpose is written by the 0A mid-term review.
2. **The TRL 4 upper bound.**
   - *Towards higher:* proponents of the Honeybee and TransAstra demos could argue TRL 4–5, treating a vacuum chamber as relevant for dehydration chemistry. That is defensible for the chemistry alone, because gravity matters little to dehydroxylation.
   - *Why I hold 3–4:* the binding risks are microgravity feed containment, capture and purification, none of which have been tested.
   - *Towards lower:* a stricter assessor would put the upper bound at 3, because the extraction demos are not documented against predictions (E8 and E9 are marked not confident).
3. **Risk class.**
   - Claude's view that water EP is the only route to an ISPP customer, if adopted, makes this architecture-change.
   - Gemini's 1,500 t/yr industrial water would also make it architecture-change, and that rate is 15–150× the pilot. At that scale this rating does not apply. The step from pilot to 1,500 t/yr would carry its own AD² of at least 5.
4. **Yield.** The 4–12 wt% recoverable figure is my assumption. Using total H₂O-equivalent (higher) halves the feed estimate. Excluding high-temperature release (to avoid SO₂/CO₂) could push it below 4%. GPT's demand for a defined yield is unmet, and the feed mass, power and tailings estimates move by ~3× on this alone.
5. **Bennu as reference feed.** An extraction pilot target is not necessarily Bennu-like. CM-like or more thermally altered C-complex NEAs would have less water and different contaminants. The rating assumes the KDP-0B target gate supplies sampled mineralogy.

## Gemini 3.1 Pro


### 1. Evidence
- **OSIRIS-REx Bennu Sample Return (2023/2024)**: Confirmed CI-chondrite composition with >10% water in hydrated phyllosilicates. Ground truth for target mineralogy, but no extraction performed.
- **Sercel et al. NIAC (2019-2022)**: Demonstrated "Optical Mining" thermal extraction on CI simulant in a vacuum chamber at ~8 kW scale. Extracted water from simulant, but microgravity handling and continuous throughput were not demonstrated.
- **Metzger et al. (2023)**: Physics-based thermal extraction model (axisymmetric Crank-Nicholson) for volatile extraction from regolith. Validated against lab data but remains an analytical model.

### 2. Current TRL
**TRL 3–4**. Analytical and experimental proof-of-concept for thermal extraction of water from simulants exists (TRL 3). Component-level lab vacuum tests have been performed (TRL 4 for specific subsystems), but integrated breadboard validation of continuous excavation, heating, and vapor capture in a relevant environment (microgravity, abrasive regolith) is incomplete. The unmet exit criterion for TRL 5 is documented test performance of a breadboard in a relevant environment with defined scaling requirements.

### 3. Target and Difficulty
**Target**: TRL 6 by KDP-0B.
**AD²**: 6. Several competing approaches exist (mechanical excavation + enclosed heating vs. optical mining/direct solar concentration), and the path to managing abrasive, cohesive regolith while capturing vapor in microgravity without massive volatile loss is not clear.

### 4. Path
1. **Sample Validation**: Lab extraction from actual Bennu/Ryugu samples to validate simulant thermal kinetics.
2. **Subsystem TVAC**: 10+ kg scale thermal vacuum extraction comparing optical vs. mechanical heating.
3. **Microgravity Handling**: Parabolic flight tests of the regolith-to-heater transfer mechanism to quantify volatile loss.
4. **0A Pathfinder**: In-space demonstrator extracting ~1-10 kg of water from a NEA.

### 5. Risk and Fallback
**Risk**: Architecture-change. If the water pilot fails or proves economically unviable, the architecture must abandon water EP and ISPP, falling back to imported Earth propellants (Iodine/Argon) for tugs.
**Fallback**: Source all propellant from Earth and abandon the water pilot, relying solely on dry metallic beneficiation for Phase 1.

### 6. Where others might disagree
The assertion that optical mining and mechanical excavation are at TRL 3-4 for this specific architecture. Proponents of optical mining may argue TRL 4-5 based on NIAC Phase III lab demonstrations, but those tests do not address the continuous 10-100 t/yr throughput and microgravity vapor capture required here.

## GPT-6.1 Sol


## T13 — Asteroid water extraction pilot

**Recommended current TRL: 2–3 for the integrated asteroid-water production system.** Laboratory extraction approaches may individually justify **TRL 3–4**, but that is not yet evidence for an autonomous **10–100 t/yr** plant operating at a C-type NEA.

**Target: TRL 6 before KDP-0B authorises the water pilot; AD² 6.** Failure is an **architecture-change** for the revised programme, not automatically project-ending for Fe-Ni production. It becomes project-ending for a water-dependent 0B option only if a signed customer makes water indispensable.

This assessment uses the revised architecture as the requirement baseline. Its October 2026 decisions are not experimental evidence, and I do not assume tests occurred after the March 2026 evidence baseline.

### 1. Define the product and feed before assigning readiness

The pilot should have an explicit purpose: **demonstrate extraction, capture, purification and storage of asteroid-derived water, and qualify it against a specified prospective customer's acceptance limits.** It is not a production LOX/LH₂ plant, and it does not establish propellant supply for the reference iodine/argon electric-propulsion tugs.

Treat its C-type site as **separate from the Fe-Ni site unless prospecting establishes a suitable shared resource**. Neither metal abundance nor accessible water follows from the other.

For assessment, I assume:

- **10–100 t/yr means net recovered, purified water**, not water initially present in processed feed.
- Feed is hydrated carbonaceous material; **free ice is not assumed**.
- Initial design envelope: **5–15 wt% thermally recoverable water equivalent**, with **50–80% end-to-end recovery**. These are engineering assumptions, not established target grades.
- Reference case: 10 wt% recoverable water and 70% recovery.
- One year of autonomous operation, including approximately **2,190 active processing hours** if processing shares a 25% duty cycle. The robot duty cycle does not necessarily constrain the processor if buffering is provided.
- Relevant environment includes vacuum, asteroid gravity, dust and fines, thermal cycling at 0.9–1.3 AU, and mission-duration radiation.

The reference case requires:

| Quantity | 10 t/yr water | 100 t/yr water |
|---|---:|---:|
| Feed processed annually | 143 t | 1,429 t |
| Water production during active processing | 4.6 kg/h | 45.7 kg/h |
| Feed processing during active processing | 65 kg/h | 652 kg/h |

Across the assumed grade/recovery envelope, annual feed demand is **83–4,000 t/yr**.

Purification must specify allowable particulates, dissolved salts, organics, sulfur-bearing species and non-condensable gases. “Water recovered” is not equivalent to “customer-qualified water.”

### 2. Evidence and demonstrated scale

| Heritage | What it supports | Demonstrated scale/environment | Required ÷ demonstrated |
|---|---|---|---|
| **OSIRIS-REx**, sample return in 2023; Lauretta et al., **“Asteroid (101955) Bennu in the laboratory: Properties of the sample collected by OSIRIS-REx,” 2024**, *Meteoritics & Planetary Science* | Hydrated minerals and chemically complex carbonaceous feed exist at an accessible NEA. | Approximately **121.6 g returned**; terrestrial sample characterisation. Not a water-production demonstration. | **n/a**: returned sample mass is not demonstrated production capacity. |
| **Hayabusa2**; Yada et al., **“Preliminary analysis of the Hayabusa2 samples returned from C-type asteroid Ryugu,” 2022**, *Nature Astronomy* | Independent evidence of hydrated carbonaceous asteroid material and heterogeneous feed properties. | Approximately **5.4 g returned**; terrestrial characterisation. | **n/a**: resource evidence, not extraction throughput. |
| **Sercel/NASA NIAC optical-mining programme, beginning in 2015**, with subsequent development reports | A formulated optical-mining process and reported terrestrial simulant experiments support an extraction proof-of-concept candidate. | Laboratory/ground simulant experiments; not sustained asteroid production. **I have not verified the supplied “8 kW” figure, recovered-water rate or test duration.** | **Not calculable** without measured net water output and operating time. Input power is not production capacity. |

**Important corrections to the inherited evidence:**

- Bennu sample results do not establish that a selected mining site supplies **10% recoverable water**. Hydration, mineralogical water equivalent and recoverable product yield are different quantities.
- Ancient brine/evaporite evidence does not demonstrate an accessible modern reservoir of liquid water or free ice.
- Economic Monte Carlo results, design studies and panel consensus contribute **no TRL credit**.
- The supplied Metzger model reference needs bibliographic and test-validation checking before being credited as validated extraction-system analysis.
- Microgravity electrolysis research is outside this pilot's extraction boundary. It cannot raise this technology's TRL, and industrial electrolysis is deferred.

### 3. Current TRL and unmet exits

| Assessment boundary | Current TRL | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---|
| Excavation → sealed thermal reactor → capture → purification → storage | **2–3** | The application is formulated. Reported laboratory work may support critical-function proof of concept, but the necessary test records are not established here. |
| Optical heating/extraction component | **3–4, conditional** | Reported physical experiments support the lower rating; TRL 4 requires documented agreement with predictions and a defined relevant environment. |
| Mechanical-feed thermal extraction route | **2–3 on the cited evidence** | Mineralogy and terrestrial heating experience support feasibility, but no qualifying integrated breadboard test has been identified here. This is an evidence limitation, not a claim that thermal processing is scientifically novel. |

**Lower-bound exit met:** TRL 2—documented application and feasible process concepts.

**For TRL 3:** obtain documented tests validating key predictions: release versus temperature/time, energy per kilogram, capture fraction and contaminant loading for representative feed.

**For TRL 4:** demonstrate an integrated laboratory breadboard with documented predictive agreement and a defined relevant environment.

**TRL 5 is not established:** no cited test demonstrates representative feed handling, release and capture together in the relevant low-gravity/vacuum environment with documented scaling requirements.

The mechanical and optical alternatives should remain separate:

- **Mechanical thermal processing:** easier to meter and characterise feed, but excavation, transfer, sealing and dust management remain critical.
- **Optical mining:** potentially reduces mechanical handling, but optical access, plume dynamics, enclosure integrity and vapor capture may dominate performance.
- There is insufficient evidence to select a winner or average their readiness.

### 4. Target, difficulty and advancement path

**Internal 0A target:** TRL 4, progressing to TRL 5 at the relevant-environment milestone.

**KDP-0B target:** TRL 6 before committing to the production pilot. No calendar date for KDP-0B is supplied. A planning allowance is **6–10 years from funded development start**, conditional on flight access and target selection.

**AD² 6:** competing approaches remain, and the complete extraction/capture architecture is unresolved. The principal difficulty is engineering integration and sustained low-gravity operation—not uncertain basic chemistry.

The following costs are **assessor-generated rough-order-of-magnitude development allowances**, not programme quotations. Activities overlap; neither durations nor costs should be mechanically summed.

| Step | Scale and acceptance evidence | Cost | Duration | Readiness reached |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Feed and customer specification | Milligram–gram returned samples/meteorites; kilogram-scale representative simulants. Measure mineralogy, release curves and contaminants; define product acceptance limits. | $1–4M | 0.5–1.5 yr | **3**, with validating experiments |
| Compare mechanical and optical breadboards | 10–100 kg feed campaigns; integrated heating, capture and purification in thermal vacuum. Validate mass/energy balances and account for water on chamber surfaces. | $5–20M | 1–2 yr | **4** |
| Relevant-environment component testing | Representative seals, feeders and capture geometry; repeated reduced-gravity tests, dusty thermal-vacuum operation, and charged-dust tests where applicable. | $10–40M | 1.5–3 yr | **5**, only where the relevant environment is actually demonstrated |
| Full-rate ground endurance and scaling validation | At least one **10 t/yr-equivalent module**, approximately 65 kg/h feed and 4.6 kg/h net water at the reference duty cycle; ≥2,000 active hours. Validate scale-out to 100 t/yr or test the larger unit. | $15–60M | 2–3 yr | **5**; terrestrial endurance alone does not establish TRL 6 |
| Integrated orbital demonstrator plus qualification campaign | Flight-representative extraction/capture module; approximately 100–500 kg representative feed for multiple campaigns at module operating rates. Combine orbital low-gravity tests with ground endurance and environmental qualification. | $150–500M | 3–5 yr | **6**, only if integrated performance and scaling predictions are validated |
| Optional NEA operational pathfinder | Extraction from actual asteroid material; measured feed, capture losses, product quality and autonomous operations. Size against the selected module, not an arbitrary kg/day benchmark. | $250–800M | 4–7 yr | **7** for the demonstrated prototype boundary |

A short orbital experiment does **not** independently establish year-long service. Conversely, TRL 6 does not necessarily require delivering a full year's product before the gate. It requires a representative prototype, relevant-environment demonstration, predictive agreement and defensible scaling—not an unvalidated extrapolation from a tiny extractor.

### 5. Risk and fallback

**Default failure classification: architecture-change.**

The revised Fe-Ni architecture does not depend on asteroid water or Phase 0 LOX/LH₂ production. Failure should therefore close or defer the water option, not automatically terminate metal production.

**Fallback:** retain 0A prospecting and extraction research; obtain any required water from Earth and operate the selected tug propellant architecture independently.

Lunar water is not an established low-risk fallback. It has its own resource, extraction, transport and qualification gates. The inherited claimed cost advantage/disadvantage is not readiness evidence.

If signed demand later makes water essential to a particular 0B option, failure becomes **project-ending for that option**, with D-02's precommitted “0A only, Earth supply” outcome.

### 6. Where assessors may disagree

1. **Integrated TRL 2–3 versus component TRL 3–4.** An assessor with access to complete optical-mining test reports could justify a higher component rating. That would not automatically raise the entire production chain.
2. **What constitutes relevant gravity.** Short reduced-gravity tests may validate individual mechanisms but not continuous feed, capture and autonomous restart.
3. **Modular scaling.** Ten qualified 10 t/yr modules could support 100 t/yr only after shared power, heat rejection, feed distribution and contamination interactions are validated.
4. **Feed assumptions.** C-type classification and hydration signatures do not establish recoverable grade or processing temperature. Sampled target grade remains a separate D-02 gate.
5. **Purpose and criticality.** Water-EP qualification may create a future customer, but it cannot be assumed to close reference transport economics or justify a water-first architecture now.

# T13 Consolidated Rating: Asteroid Water Extraction Pilot (`isru-water-extraction`)

**Rapporteur's note.** This consolidates three assessments: Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-6.1 Sol. Every claim is attributed to the model that made it. Where models diverge, the divergence is recorded together with the source or test that would resolve it. No position is adopted.

---

## 1. Summary of ratings

| | Claude Opus 5.5 | Gemini 3.1 Pro | GPT-6.1 Sol |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Current TRL** | 3–4. Dehydration chemistry 3→4; integrated chain "3 at best" | 3–4. Some subsystems at 4 | 2–3 integrated. Optical component 3–4 (conditional); mechanical route 2–3 |
| **TRL exit met (lower bound)** | TRL 3 | TRL 3 | TRL 2 only |
| **Target at KDP-0B** | TRL 5. Rises to 6 if rq-0-55 selects water EP | TRL 6 | TRL 6, with an internal 0A target of TRL 4→5 |
| **AD²** | 5. Would be 6 for a step to TRL 6 | 6 | 6 |
| **Risk if it fails** | Cost-increase. Architecture-change if water EP is adopted | Architecture-change | Architecture-change. Project-ending for an option only if a signed customer makes water indispensable |
| **Years to target** | 3–6 | 5–8 | 6–10 (from funded start; date of KDP-0B unspecified) |
| **Phase need** | 0B (conditional). Would accept "deferred" if no purpose is written by the 0A mid-term review | 0B | 0B |
| **Required duration (assumed)** | ≥1 yr continuous within a 3–5 yr site life | 1.5–5 yr | 1 yr; ~2,190 active hours at 25% duty |
| **Self-rated confidence** | Medium | Medium | Medium |

---

## 2. Where the models agree

**On what the evidence shows (all three):**
- The Bennu (and, for Claude and GPT, Ryugu) returned samples are evidence about the **resource**. They are not evidence of extraction.
- Microgravity feed handling, containment and vapour capture have **not been demonstrated**. Continuous throughput at pilot scale has not been demonstrated either.
- Mechanical excavation with enclosed heating and optical mining are **competing approaches with no demonstrated winner**.
- A thermal-vacuum bench extractor in the tens-of-kg class, comparing the two routes, is the next major ground step. The stated cost is $5–20M (Claude, GPT) or $5–15M (Gemini).
- Fallback: Fe-Ni production proceeds. Any water needed comes from Earth, and the tugs remain on imported propellant. Gemini frames this as abandoning water EP and ISPP; Claude and GPT frame it as the iodine/argon reference already being the baseline (D-05).

**Claude and GPT agree (Gemini does not address these points):**
- The rating boundary excludes electrolysis, LOX/LH₂ and thrusters. Rq-0-33 cannot raise this TRL.
- The feed is water bound in hydrated minerals. Free ice is not assumed.
- Hydration or mineralogical water content is not the same as recoverable yield.
- A C-type pilot is probably on a **separate site** from the Fe-Ni plant, unless prospecting shows otherwise.
- The **pilot purpose and product purity specification are undefined**, and this blocks a defined relevant environment.
- The Paper 05 Monte Carlo, other design studies and panel decisions earn **no TRL credit**.
- **Lunar polar water is not a meaningful fallback** under the revised architecture.
- Short parabolic or drop-tower tests are too short to validate continuous feed, heat-up, capture and restart.
- No 0B baseline element depends on water. The two models then classify the risk differently (see §3.3).

---

## 3. Where the models diverge, and why

### 3.1 Current TRL: Claude 3–4 and Gemini 3–4, versus GPT 2–3 (integrated)

| Model | Basis |
|---|---|
| **Claude** | TRL 3 is met because Garenne et al. 2014 TGA validates the key parameter (water release versus temperature) on real meteorites. Simulant work (Britt 2019) and small vacuum demos (Honeybee WINE, Sercel APIS) support this, though Claude marks both demos as not confident. The upper bound of 4 holds only if those demos are accepted as breadboard validation of extraction alone. |
| **Gemini** | Sercel NIAC optical mining (marked confident: ~8 kW, ~1–10 kg batches). Metzger et al. 2023 is described as "validated against lab data". |
| **GPT** | TRL 3 requires validated predictions of release versus temperature and time, energy per kg, **capture fraction and contaminant loading** on representative feed. GPT has not established these test records. The optical-mining figures are unverified. |

**Root of the divergence.** The models apply different definitions of the TRL 3 "key parameters":
- Claude treats release versus temperature as sufficient.
- GPT requires capture and contaminant data as well.

The models also give different credence to the same optical-mining record. Claude's integrated-chain rating ("3 at best") and GPT's (2–3) overlap more than the headline ranges suggest.

**What would settle it:**
1. A panel ruling on which parameters count as "key" for the TRL 3 exit of this chain.
2. Retrieval of the Sercel/APIS and Honeybee WINE test reports. These would need to show measured water captured, run duration, power, and agreement with prior predictions.
3. Verification of the Metzger reference: authorship, arXiv ID, and whether it was validated against test data.

### 3.2 Target TRL at KDP-0B: Claude 5, versus Gemini and GPT 6

| Model | Reasoning |
|---|---|
| **Claude** | Under D-02 the pilot is not project-ending, so the internal-milestone band of 4–5 applies. Claude sets the top of that band because KDP-0B commits a flight pilot. The pilot itself then serves as the TRL 6–7 demonstration. |
| **GPT** | TRL 6 is required *before* committing to the production pilot. |
| **Gemini** | TRL 6, with no stated derivation. |

**Nature of the divergence.** This is an interpretation of programme policy, not a disagreement about evidence. AD² follows from it: Claude rates AD² 6 for a step to TRL 6, which matches the other two models.

**What would settle it:**
- A programme ruling on how D-02 applies to a pilot that is itself a flight demonstration.
- The outcome of rq-0-55. Claude's escalation clause raises the target to 6 if water EP is selected.

### 3.3 Risk class: Claude cost-increase, versus Gemini and GPT architecture-change

- **Claude and GPT share the factual premise** that no 0B baseline element depends on water. They label the consequence differently:
  - Claude: the loss is option value, so the class is cost-increase.
  - GPT: failure closes or defers the water option, which counts as an architecture change.
- **Gemini's premise differs.** Gemini states that failure would force the architecture to "abandon water EP and ISPP". Claude and GPT treat neither as part of the 0B baseline.

**What would settle it:**
- The rq-0-55 outcome. Claude moves to architecture-change if water EP enters Phase 1 transport.
- A programme definition of whether closing an optional element counts as an architecture change.

### 3.4 Years to target: 3–6, 5–8 and 6–10

These figures follow from the target (TRL 5 versus 6) and from path content:
- GPT includes full-rate ground endurance and an orbital prototype as required steps.
- Claude makes the equivalents conditional or optional.

Resolving §3.2 largely resolves this.

### 3.5 Yield and feed assumptions

| Model | Recoverable water | Recovery factor | Feed mass |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude | 4–12 wt% | (included in yield) | ~80–2,500 t/yr |
| GPT | 5–15 wt% | 50–80% | 83–4,000 t/yr envelope; 143–1,429 t/yr reference case |
| Gemini | ">10% water" in Bennu, stated as confirmed | — | not derived |

- Claude and GPT both label their figures as assumptions.
- Claude notes that feed mass, power and tailings move by about 3× on the yield assumption alone.

**What would settle it:**
- Evolved-gas and TGA data on returned Bennu and Ryugu material that distinguish recoverable water from total water, with co-released species measured.
- The sampled mineralogy of the selected target, through the D-02 target gate.

### 3.6 Placement of the in-space demonstrator

| Model | In-space step | Status | Stated cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude | kg-scale payload on a C-type rendezvous scout | Optional | $50–150M incremental |
| Gemini | 0A pathfinder extracting 1–10 kg of water | Required for TRL 6 | $150–300M |
| GPT | Orbital prototype with 100–500 kg feed campaigns | Required for TRL 6 | $150–500M |
| GPT | NEA operational pathfinder | Optional, for TRL 7 | $250–800M |

This placement depends on the target-TRL ruling in §3.2.

### 3.7 Gemini's sample-extraction step

Gemini assigns TRL 4 to lab extraction from Bennu or Ryugu samples. Claude and GPT treat equivalent mg-to-gram sample work as firming TRL 3 only. This is the same disagreement about exit criteria as §3.1.

### 3.8 Cross-reference to check

Claude's §6 refers to "Gemini's 1,500 t/yr industrial water" and to "Claude's view that water EP is the only route to an ISPP customer". Neither appears in the Gemini or Claude submissions considered here. They appear to refer to earlier-round inputs and should not be attributed to these assessments without confirmation.

---

## 4. Evidence cited

| Evidence | Cited by | Flags |
|---|---|---|
| **Lauretta et al. 2024, *MAPS*: Bennu sample properties** | Claude, GPT. Gemini cites OSIRIS-REx generally. | Mass is ~120 g (Claude) or ~121.6 g (GPT). Gemini's ">10% water" is marked unverified by Claude, and GPT states hydration ≠ recoverable yield. |
| **Ryugu sample, ~5.4 g** | Claude (Yokoyama et al. 2023, *Science*); GPT (Yada et al. 2022, *Nature Astronomy*) | Each paper is cited by **one model only**. They agree on substance. |
| **Garenne et al. 2014, *GCA*: TGA of CI/CM/CR chondrites** | Claude only | **Single-model.** This is Claude's main basis for TRL 3 being met. |
| **Sercel et al., NASA NIAC optical mining** | All three | **Inconsistent and partly unsure.** Claude dates it ~2016–2019 and is unsure of scale and power. GPT dates it from 2015 and is unsure of 8 kW, output and duration. Gemini dates it 2019–2022, is confident in ~8 kW and ~1–10 kg, and alone cites Phase III. |
| **Metzger et al. (2023; arXiv 2306.03776 per Claude)** | Claude, Gemini, GPT | Claude is unsure of authorship and ID and omits it from the YAML. GPT says it needs bibliographic and validation checking. Gemini is confident and says it was "validated against lab data". |
| Honeybee Robotics / UCF WINE, ~2018–2019 | Claude only | **Single-model; marked unsure** on mass and rate. |
| McCoy et al. 2025, *Nature*: Bennu evaporites | Claude only | **Single-model.** GPT separately notes that evaporite evidence does not imply accessible liquid water or ice. |
| Glavin et al. 2025, *Nat. Astron.*: Bennu NH₃ and organics | Claude only | **Single-model; marked unsure** on the March "more volatile-rich than Ryugu" framing. |
| Lauretta et al. 2022 (*Science*); Walsh et al. 2022 (*Sci. Adv.*): Bennu TAG response | Claude only | Single-model. Bears on feed acquisition design. |
| Britt et al. 2019, *MAPS*: CI/CM simulants | Claude only | Single-model. Representativeness for organics, NH₃ and salts is Claude's judgement. |
| ISS Water Recovery System | Claude only | Single-model. Feed chemistry differs from this application. |
| MOXIE (Hecht 2021; Hoffman 2022) | Claude only | Single-model. Indirect operations heritage only. |
| Romero-Calvo et al. 2025, *Nat. Chem.* | Claude only | Single-model. Claude marks it out of scope. |
| "TransAstra demos" | Claude (§6, in passing) | No citation given. |

**Highest-weight items confirmed by more than one model:**
- The Bennu and Ryugu sample characterisations, which are resource evidence only.

**Items that bear most on the TRL and are unresolved:**
- The optical-mining test record.
- The Metzger model.
- Garenne 2014, if the panel accepts release versus temperature as the key parameter.

---

## 5. Consolidated path

Steps are merged where the models describe equivalent work. Each model's cost, duration and "reaches TRL" figures are kept separate. GPT states that its costs and durations overlap and should not be summed.

| # | Step | Claude | Gemini | GPT |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Define pilot purpose, yield target and product purity specification** | P1: $0.5–2M, 0.5–1 yr; prerequisite for TRL 4 | Not included | Combined with step 2: $1–4M, 0.5–1.5 yr → TRL 3 |
| 2 | **Characterise feed on meteorites and returned samples**: release curves and contaminant model (H₂O, CO₂, SO₂/H₂S, NH₃, organics, salts) | P2: mg scale, Bennu allocation request; $0.3–1.5M, 1–2 yr → TRL 3 (firmed) | Bennu/Ryugu lab extraction: grams; $1–3M, 1–2 yr → **TRL 4** | mg–g samples plus kg simulants (see step 1) → TRL 3 |
| 3 | **Develop representative simulant** (organics, sulfur phases, evaporites) | P3: 100 kg–1 t batches; $1–4M, 1–2 yr | Not included | Included in step 1 |
| 4 | **Thermal-vacuum bench extractor, mechanical versus optical**: closed mass balance, condensate speciation, fines carryover | P4: 10–50 kg/day; $5–20M, 2–3 yr → TRL 4 | 10–50 kg/day; $5–15M, 2–3 yr → **TRL 5** | 10–100 kg feed campaigns, including capture and purification; $5–20M, 1–2 yr → TRL 4 |
| 5 | **Purification breadboard** against the specification, on real-chemistry condensate | P5: 0.1–1 t/yr water; $2–8M, 1–2 yr → TRL 4 | Not included | Folded into step 4 |
| 6 | **Reduced-gravity handling, sealing and vapour capture** | P6: parabolic or drop tower, then ISS or free-flyer over weeks; $10–60M, 2–4 yr → TRL 5 | Parabolic flight (in text, not in YAML) | Reduced gravity, dusty vacuum, charged dust; $10–40M, 1.5–3 yr → TRL 5 |
| 7 | **Validated model and documented scaling requirements** | P7: $0.5–2M, 1 yr in parallel → TRL 5 exit documentation | Not included | Folded into step 8 |
| 8 | **Ground endurance and scaling validation** | P8, only if escalated to TRL 6: 0.1–1 t/day feed, ≥1,000 h; $50–200M, 3–5 yr → TRL 6 | Not included | Required: 10 t/yr-equivalent module (~65 kg/h feed), ≥2,000 active h; $15–60M, 2–3 yr → TRL 5 (endurance alone does not give 6) |
| 9 | **In-space demonstrator** | P9, optional: C-type scout payload, kg to tens of kg; $50–150M incremental, 4–7 yr → 6–7 at small scale | Required 0A pathfinder: 1–10 kg; $150–300M, 3–5 yr → TRL 6 | Required orbital prototype: 100–500 kg feed; $150–500M, 3–5 yr → TRL 6 |
